nameStory: Wild rosemary gets its name from its narrow, evergreen leaves that look remarkably similar to the culinary herb rosemary, though they're not related at all. It's also called bog-rosemary because it lives exclusively in soggy, acidic bogs. The scientific name Andromeda comes from Greek mythology - the princess chained to a rock, much like how this delicate plant is 'chained' to its harsh bog habitat.
description: Wild rosemary is a low-growing evergreen shrub that rarely reaches more than a foot tall. It has narrow, leathery leaves that are dark green on top and silvery-white underneath, giving the plant a distinctive two-toned appearance. In late spring and early summer, it produces small, bell-shaped pink or white flowers that dangle delicately from the stems. This hardy little shrub is perfectly adapted to life in cold, wet, acidic bogs where few other plants can survive.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, needle-like evergreen leaves about 1-2 inches long with rolled edges. Dark green on top, bright silvery-white underneath - flip a leaf over for the telltale flash of silver.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, bell-shaped flowers that hang downward like tiny pink or white lanterns. They feel papery and delicate, blooming in clusters at branch tips in late spring.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading evergreen shrub typically 6-12 inches tall. Forms small colonies through underground runners, creating patches in the bog.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, woody stems that are often reddish-brown. Young twigs feel slightly fuzzy to the touch and may have a waxy coating.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds. Capsules persist into winter, turning brown and papery.

habitat: Found exclusively in cold, acidic sphagnum bogs and boggy areas throughout northern New England. Prefers constantly moist, nutrient-poor peat soils with pH levels that would kill most other plants. Often grows alongside cranberries, pitcher plants, and various sedges in these specialized wetland communities.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges bright green, contrasting with older silvery foliage. Flower buds begin to swell in late spring, preparing for the upcoming bloom period.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in early to mid-summer with drooping pink or white bell-shaped blooms. The silvery undersides of leaves are most prominent as summer heat makes them curl slightly.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and split open to release seeds. Foliage remains evergreen but may take on slightly deeper green tones as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves provide year-round identification, though they may appear more tightly curled in cold weather. Dried seed capsules often persist, rattling softly in winter winds.

funFact: Wild rosemary is one of the few plants that can actually thrive in water with the acidity level of vinegar - its bog homes are so acidic they would burn your skin if you stayed in contact too long!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Labrador tea, which also grows in bogs and has silvery leaf undersides. However, Labrador tea has much wider, oval leaves with fuzzy brown (not bright silver) undersides, and its leaves have a spicy fragrance when crushed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, wild rosemary is completely unrelated to culinary rosemary and should never be used for cooking - it contains toxic compounds. The name confusion has led to occasional poisoning incidents when foragers mistake it for the edible herb.
compareHints: Wild rosemary is the only species in its genus Andromeda, making it unique in New England. Within the heath family, it's most similar to other bog shrubs like leatherleaf and bog laurel, but those have wider leaves without the distinctive bright silvery undersides. Its needle-like evergreen leaves and exclusive bog habitat make it quite distinctive once you know what to look for.
